newsitem.title: GERMANY: NATO's Solana hopes for full Bosnia force in 1997.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana hopes for full Bosnia force in 1997.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said on Wednesday he hoped all 33 countries taking part in a NATO-led peace Implementation Force in Bosnia would agree to join a follow-on force after the current mandate expires.

Speaking to reporters in Bonn after talks with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, Solana also expressed his hope that NATO itself, and not Russia, would decide on any future expansion of the security organisation.
"I do hope that all the countries that cooperated in Bosnia in 1996 will continue to cooperate in 1997," Solana said. "We have 33 countries there now. I do hope they will all continue in 1997."
NATO has an obligation, he said, to help cement the peace and reconstruction of Bosnia.

Solana said NATO owed Germany a debt of gratitude for contributing soldiers to peacekeeping efforts in the past year. "You are prepared to continue with forces on the ground in Bosnia. This is a very positive and very important decision."
Solana did not specifically mention the United States, but Kinkel said he was confident U.S. forces would be part of a new mission after the current IFOR mandate expires in December.
"Germany would very much welcome the American continuation in Bosnia," Kinkel said. "I assume there will be a positive decision on that."

NATO sources said last month the alliance would soon present plans to commit thousands of troops to Bosnia after the mandate expires. They said the 18 non-NATO countries in IFOR had expressed no objections to staying on in a new mission.
Any new peace force is expected to number several thousand below the 58,000-strong mission sent to oversee implementation of the December 1995 Dayton peace accords which ended Bosnia's 43-month war.
Solana said he would not address any specific criticism of possible NATO expansion plans.

"The important thing to know is that we are prepared, and we wish to construct a solid, profound and healthy relationship between NATO and Russia," he said. "It is important for Russia and it is important for NATO. But no one is going to stop us."
